01 | Functions of the Kidneys | The kidneys are both regulatory and excretory organs, performing five major functions essential for homeostasis.

Section 01 | Functions of the Kidneys | The kidneys are both regulatory and excretory organs. | 1 | Regulation of | body fluid osmolarity and volume | . | 2 | Regulation of | electrolyte balance | . | 3 | Regulation of | acid-base balance | . | 4 | Excretion of metabolic products | and foreign substances. | 5 | Production and secretion of hormones | . | Key Concept | Regulatory functions (fluid, electrolytes, acid-base) work together with the excretory function (metabolic waste and foreign substances) — plus an endocrine role through production and secretion of hormones.
02 | Gross Anatomy of the Kidney | The medial side of each kidney contains an indentation through which pass the renal artery, vein, nerves and pelvis.

Section 02 | Gross Anatomy — The Kidney | Figure (1): structure of the human kidney | On the cut surface of a bisected kidney two regions are evident: an outer | cortex | and an inner | medulla | . | The cortex and medulla are composed of | nephrons | — the functional units of the kidney. | The | pelvis | represents the upper expanded region of the | ureter | , which carries urine from the pelvis to the urinary bladder. | The pelvis divides into two or three open-ended pouches, the | major calyces | , that divide into | minor calyces | . | Figure (1): structure of the human kidney | Kidney | Calyces | Renal pelvis | Renal artery | Renal vein | Medulla | Ureter | Cortex
03 | Ultra-structure of the Nephron | The first step in urine formation begins with the ultra filtration of plasma across the glomerular capillaries (i.e., glomerulus).

Section 03 | Ultra-structure of the Nephron — Renal Corpuscle | Figure (2): Ultra structure of the renal corpuscle | The term | ultra filtration | refers to the passive movement of an essentially | protein-free fluid | from the glomerular capillaries into | Bowman's space | . | The glomerulus is a network of capillaries supplied by the | afferent arteriole | and drained by the | efferent arteriole | . | Capillaries are covered by epithelial cells called | podocytes | , forming the | visceral layer | of Bowman's capsule. | The visceral cells are reflected at the | vascular pole | to form the | parietal layer | of Bowman's capsule. | The space between both layers is | Bowman's space | , which at the | urinary pole | becomes the lumen of the | proximal tubule | . | Schematic: renal corpuscle & tubules | Diagram labels — Figure (2) | (a): | Pores in endothelium, Capillary lumen, Glomerulus, Pedicels of podocytes, Lamina densa, Filtration slit, Capsular space | (c): | Capillary, Capillary endothelium, Basement membrane, Foot processes of podocyte of glomerular capsule, Filtration slit, Slit diaphragm, Filtrate in capsular space, Foot processes of podocyte, Plasma, Fenestration

Section 03 | The Glomerular Filtration Barrier | Capillary endothelium, basement membrane and foot processes of podocytes form the filtration barrier | The | endothelial cells | of glomerular capillaries are covered by a | basement membrane | , which is surrounded by | podocytes | . | The capillary endothelium, basement membrane and foot processes of podocytes form the so-called | filtration barrier | . | The endothelium is | fenestrated | and is | freely permeable | to water and to small solutes such as | urea | and | glucose | — and even to small protein molecules. | Slit diaphragms bridge the filtration slits between the foot processes. | Filtration barrier: fenestrated endothelium → basement membrane → podocytes | Related figures | Figure 2: Renal corpuscle and the juxtaglomerular apparatus • Figure 3: E/M podocytes and glomerular capillary.
04 | Glomerular Filtration | The glomerular network of specialized capillaries serves as the filtering mechanism of the kidney.

Section 04 | The Glomerular Filtration (Ultrafiltration) | What passes through — and what is held back — by the glomerular filter | The ultra filtrate (cell-free) contains | Electrolytes, glucose, phosphate, urea, creatinine, peptides, low molecular weight proteins | — all the substances in the plasma. The filtrate is collected in Bowman space and enters the tubules, where its composition is modified with body needs until it leaves the kidney as urine. | Excluded from the filtrate | Proteins having | molecular weight exceeding 68,000 | , such as | albumin and globulin | . The ultra filtrate is therefore essentially protein-free (cell-free). | Fetal life | During the fetal life, the | placenta | serves as the major excretory organ.

Wrap-Up | Key Takeaways | The kidneys are | regulatory and excretory | organs: fluid/osmolarity, electrolytes, acid-base, waste excretion and hormone production. | Gross anatomy: outer | cortex | , inner | medulla | , | pelvis | dividing into major and minor | calyces | , draining via the | ureter | . | The | nephron | is the functional unit; the renal corpuscle (glomerulus + Bowman's capsule) starts urine formation by | ultrafiltration | . | The | filtration barrier | = fenestrated endothelium + basement membrane + podocyte foot processes. | Ultrafiltrate is protein-free except molecules ≤ 68,000 MW; the placenta is the major excretory organ in fetal life. | Next topic: Changes in the Colour of Urine — the diagnostic approach to red/brown urine. | Source: Pediatric Renal Book 4th Grade — Prof. Dr. Mohamed Bahbah & Prof. Dr. Ghada Al-Mashad (pp. 55-58)

01 | Causes of Urine Colour Changes | The colour of urine can give a diagnostic clue to the underlying cause or disease.

Section 01 | Causes of Urine Colour Changes | Three characteristic colour changes and their causes | White Milky Urine | Pus | Phosphate crystals | Chylous | Green Urine | Pseudomonas infection | Food with excess chlorophyll | Dark Yellow Urine | ↑ Bilirubin | Concentrated urine

Section 02 | General Principles | Normal range and the meaning of colour change | Normal urine colour | The colour of normal urine may range from | yellow or almost colourless | to | amber yellow | , depending on the amount of fluid intake and the type of eaten foods. | Why does urine colour change? | Changes in urine colour can be | simply caused by ingestion of certain foods, drinks or drugs | — or may | reflect several diseases of different origins | . | The most common pathological causes | Hematuria, bilirubinuria and hemoglobinuria | are the most common. The colour of urine can give a | diagnostic clue | to the underlying cause or disease.
02 | Dark Red / Brown Urine | Diagnostic approach: centrifuge the urine, use the dipstick heme test, and distinguish macroscopic from microscopic hematuria.

Section 03 | Stepwise Diagnostic Approach — Part 1 | Causes of dark red or brown urine — centrifuge result and dipstick heme | Centrifuge result of urine | Supernatant red | Sediment red | = without RBCs | = with RBCs (Hematuria) | Dipstick heme | HEME-POSITIVE | HEME-NEGATIVE | ✓ Hemoglobinuria | Drugs | ✓ Myoglobinuria | Dyes | Macroscopic vs Microscopic | Macroscopic | Microscopic | Pink or red (gross hematuria) | Normal

Section 03 | Heme-Positive — Hemoglobinuria vs Myoglobinuria | Two conditions that give a positive dipstick heme test | 1. Hemoglobinuria | With | acute hemolytic anemia | . | CBC shows | fragmented RBCs & reticulocytosis | . | Hemoglobin in urine | . | Plasma color red | . | 2. Myoglobinuria | Due to | rhabdomyolysis | (skeletal muscle injury) in viral myositis, crush, prolonged fits. | High serum creatine kinase | . | Plasma color clear | . | Key discriminating point | Both give | red/brown urine | with a | positive dipstick heme | — the plasma color (red in hemoglobinuria vs clear in myoglobinuria) and CBC findings (fragmented RBCs & reticulocytosis) help differentiate the two.

Section 03 | Heme-Negative — Drugs, Dyes & Others | Red/brown urine with a NEGATIVE dipstick heme test | Drugs (a–k) | Chloroquine | Deferoxamine | Ibuprofen | Iron sorbitol | Metronidazole | Nitrofurantoin | Phenazopyridine (Pyridium) | Phenolphthalein | Rifampin | Salicylates | Sulfasalazine | Dyes (vegetable / fruit) | Beets, blackberries, food coloring. | Other causes | Methemoglobin | and | Urates | .

Wrap-Up | Key Takeaways | Urine colour ranges from | colourless to amber yellow | depending on fluid intake and foods; changes may be dietary/drug-related or disease-related. | White milky urine → pus, phosphate crystals, chylous; green urine → Pseudomonas, excess chlorophyll; dark yellow → bilirubin, concentrated urine. | For dark red/brown urine: | centrifuge | (supernatant red = no RBCs; sediment red = hematuria) and | dipstick heme | test. | Heme-positive | : hemoglobinuria (acute hemolytic anemia, fragmented RBCs, red plasma) or myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis, high CK, clear plasma). | Heme-negative | : 11 drugs (chloroquine → sulfasalazine), vegetable/fruit dyes, methemoglobin and urates. | Next topic: Hematuria — definitions, causes and evaluation in children. | Source: Pediatric Renal Book 4th Grade — Prof. Dr. Mohamed Bahbah & Prof. Dr. Ghada Al-Mashad (pp. 58-59)

01 | Definition | Hematuria: presence of blood in urine — gross (visible to the naked eye) or microscopic (detected only by dipstick or microscopy).

Section 01 | Definition of Hematuria | Hematuria | Presence of | blood in urine | . It may be | gross | (visible to naked eye) or | microscopic | (detected only by dipstick or microscopy). | Microscopic hematuria | Defined as | more than 5 RBCs per high power field | in the sediment from | 10 ml of centrifuged freshly voided urine | . | Macroscopic hematuria | Grossly visible blood — appears | pink or red | (and cola or smoky when of glomerular origin).
02 | Causes of Hematuria in Children | Hematuria is divided into glomerular and extra-glomerular (upper and lower urinary tract) causes.

Section 02 | Causes of Hematuria — Glomerular & Upper Tract (1/2) | Glomerular Hematuria — Isolated Renal Disease | IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) | Post-infectious GN (i.e., post-streptococcal GN) | Membranous nephropathy | Membrano-proliferative GN | Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis | Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease | Glomerular Hematuria — Multi-system Disease | Systemic lupus erythematosus nephritis | Henoch–Schönlein purpura nephritis | Good-pasture syndrome | Hemolytic-uremic syndrome | Sickle cell glomerulopathy | HIV nephropathy | Extra Glomerular — Upper urinary tract | Tubulointerstitial: | Pyelonephritis, Interstitial nephritis, Acute tubular necrosis • | Vascular: | Arterial/venous thrombosis, Malformations (aneurysms, hemangiomas)

Section 02 | Causes of Hematuria — Extra-Glomerular (2/2) | Crystalluria | Calcium, Oxalate, Uric acid | Anatomical | Cystic kidney disease, Poly-cystic kidney disease, Multi-cystic dysplasia, Tumor (Wilms), Trauma | Lower urinary tract | Cystitis, Urethritis, Urolithiasis | Summary of the classification | Glomerular hematuria → isolated renal disease or multi-system disease. Extra-glomerular hematuria → upper urinary tract (tubulointerstitial, vascular, crystalluria, anatomical) or lower urinary tract (cystitis, urethritis, urolithiasis).

Section 02 | Common Causes of Gross Hematuria | Extra-Glomerular | Urinary tract infection | Meatal stenosis | Perineal irritation | Trauma | Urolithiasis / hypercalciuria | Coagulopathy | Tumor | Glomerular | IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) | Alport syndrome (hereditary nephritis) | Thin glomerular basement membrane nephropathy | Post-infectious GN (i.e., post-streptococcal GN) | Henoch–Schönlein purpura nephritis | Systemic lupus erythematosus nephritis | Recurrent gross hematuria | Recurrent gross H — consider IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) in particular.
03 | Evaluation of the Child with Hematuria | Evaluation begins with a careful history, physical examination, and laboratory investigations.

Section 03 | Evaluation of the Child with Hematuria | A | careful history | , | Physical examination | , | Laboratory investigations | . | Purpose of this information | Used to determine the | level of hematuria | (i.e., upper or lower urinary tract) and to determine the | urgency of the evaluation | based on the symptomatology. | Special consideration | Given to | family history | , identification of | anatomic abnormalities / malformation syndromes | , and the presence of | gross hematuria | .

Section 03 | Renal vs Urinary Tract Hematuria | Q. How can you differentiate renal from urinary tract hematuria? | Feature | Renal Hematuria (Glomerular and upper urinary tract) | Urinary Tract Hematuria (lower urinary tract) | Source | Nephron (i.e., glomerulus, convoluted / collecting tubules and interstitium) | Pelvicalyceal system, ureter, bladder, or urethra. | Color | Cola or smoky | Pink or red (gross hematuria) | RBCs | Deformed (dysmorphic) | Normal | RBCs Casts | + | − | Blood Clots | − | + | Proteinuria (dipstick) | Exceeding 100 mg/dL | Minimal | c/p | Oedema, hypertension | Dysuria
04 | Approach to Diagnosis | A structured clinical and laboratory approach: localize the hematuria, then search for the cause.

Section 04 | Clinical Approach to Diagnosis | Is this red urine | “hematuria” | ? | What are the | causes | of hematuria? | Clinical approach | of hematuria: search for signs suggestive of each cause. | Laboratory approach | of hematuria: | localize hematuria | (glomerular or extraglomerular). | For all cases | Analysis of | fresh urine sample | for casts, bacteria, crystals, RBCs shape. | Abdominal ultrasound | for stones, tumors, malformations. | Renal functions tests | . | Blood picture | . | Coagulation profile | .

Section 04 | Laboratory Approach by Site of Hematuria | For Glomerular hematuria — reduced C3 in | Post infectious glomerulonephritis. | Systemic lupus nephritis. | Nephritis with chronic infection. | Membrano proliferative glomerulonephritis. | For post-streptococcal GN | ASO titre. | Anti DNase titre. | Throat or skin culture. | For lupus nephritis | ANA. | Anti Double strand DNA. | For extra glomerular hematuria | Urine culture for urinary tract infections. | 24 hours urine Calcium, uric acid & oxalate for Crystalluria, stones. | Cystogram & renal scan for hydronephrosis. | Renal Doppler for renal vein thrombosis.

Section 04 | Renal Biopsy — Indications | # | Indication for renal biopsy | 1 | Unexplained persistent or recurrent gross hematuria. | 2 | Lupus nephritis. | 3 | Glomerulonephritis with: Nephritic nephrosis or absent low C3. | 4 | Unexplained acute renal failure.

Wrap-Up | Key Takeaways | Hematuria = blood in urine; | microscopic | = > 5 RBCs/HPF in sediment from 10 ml of centrifuged freshly voided urine. | Causes: | glomerular | (isolated renal disease or multi-system disease) vs | extra-glomerular | (upper and lower urinary tract). | Common gross hematuria: extra-glomerular (UTI, trauma, urolithiasis, coagulopathy, tumor) vs glomerular (IgA nephropathy, Alport, PSGN, HSP, SLE). | Differentiate by: color (cola/smoky vs pink/red), RBCs (dysmorphic vs normal), casts, clots, proteinuria, and clinical picture. | Workup: localize first — C3, ASO/DNase, ANA/dsDNA for glomerular; culture, 24-hr calcium/urate/oxalate, cystogram, Doppler for extra-glomerular. | Renal biopsy: unexplained persistent/recurrent gross hematuria, lupus nephritis, GN with nephritic nephrosis or absent low C3, unexplained ARF. | Next topic: Acute Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (APSGN). | Source: Pediatric Renal Book 4th Grade — Prof. Dr. Mohamed Bahbah & Prof. Dr. Ghada Al-Mashad (pp. 59-67)

Pediatric Nephrology | Table of Contents | Source: Pediatric Renal Book 4th Grade — Prof. Dr. Mohamed Bahbah & Prof. Dr. Ghada Al-Mashad (pp. 67-69) | 01 | Definition | 02 | Etiology & Epidemiology | 03 | Pathogenesis & Pathology | 04 | Clinical Manifestations | 05 | Complications & Medical Emergencies | 06 | Diagnosis | 07 | Differential Diagnosis & Prevention | 08 | Treatment | 09 | Prognosis | 10 | Key Takeaways
01 | Definition | Acute specific self-limited glomerulonephritis due to prior streptococcal infection.

Section 01 | Definition of APSGN | Definition | Acute | specific, self-limited glomerulonephritis | due to | prior streptococcal infection | , characterized by four cardinal features: | 1 | Sudden onset of | gross hematuria | 2 | Edema ( | mild to moderate | ) | 3 | Hypertension | 4 | Oliguria | — may be present
02 | Etiology & Epidemiology | APSGN follows infection of the throat or skin by certain nephritogenic strains of group A β-hemolytic streptococci.

Section 02 | Etiology & Epidemiology | Throat vs skin infection — nephritogenic strains and differences | AGN after throat infection | AGN after skin infection | Strain of strept. | Type 4, 12 | Type 49 | Season | Winter and spring | Summer | Latent period | 1–2 weeks | 2–3 weeks | ASO titre | Elevated | May be normal | Key teaching point | The | latent period | (1–2 wk throat, 2–3 wk skin) and the | ASO titre | behavior differ between throat and skin infections — ASO is commonly elevated after pharyngeal infection but rarely after skin infection.
03 | Pathogenesis & Pathology | Morphologic studies and the depression in serum complement (C3) strongly suggest an immune-complex-mediated mechanism.

Section 03 | Pathogenesis — Immune Complex Mediated | Mechanism | Although morphologic studies and a depression in the | serum complement (C3) level | strongly suggest that PSGN is mediated by | immune complexes | , the precise mechanisms by which nephritogenic streptococci induce complex formation remain to be determined. | Streptococcal infection | → | Abs → Ag–Ab + complement (C3) immune complexes | → | Deposited in GBM (subepithelial humps) | → | Edema, Hypertension, Oliguria

Section 03 | Pathology of APSGN | Gross & light microscopy | The kidneys appear | symmetrically enlarged | . On light microscopy, all glomeruli appear | enlarged and relatively bloodless | and show | diffuse mesangial cell proliferation | with an increase in mesangial matrix. | Immunofluorescence microscopy | Reveals | lumpy bumpy deposits | of immunoglobulin and complement on the | glomerular basement membrane (GBM) | and in the mesangium. | Electron microscopy | Electron-dense deposits, or | “humps” | , are observed on the | epithelial side of the GBM | .
04 | Clinical Manifestations | Age 5–12 yr; uncommon before the age of 3 yr. Acute nephritic syndrome follows the streptococcal infection.

Section 04 | Clinical Manifestations | Age: | 5–12 yr and uncommon before the age of 3 yr. | The typical patient develops an | acute nephritic syndrome | 1–2 wk after an antecedent | streptococcal pharyngitis | or | 3–6 wk after a streptococcal pyoderma | . | The severity of renal involvement varies from | asymptomatic microscopic hematuria | with normal renal function to | acute kidney injury | . | Depending on the severity, patients may develop various degrees of | edema, hypertension, and oliguria | . | Patients may develop | encephalopathy and/or heart failure | owing to hypertension or hypervolemia; encephalopathy may also result directly from toxic effects of the streptococcal bacteria on the CNS. | Edema | typically results from salt and water retention. | Nonspecific symptoms: | malaise, lethargy, abdominal or flank pain, and fever | .

Section 04 | Course & Complications | Natural course | The | acute phase generally resolves within 6–8 wk | . Although urinary protein excretion and hypertension usually normalize by | 6 wk | after onset, persistent | microscopic hematuria may persist for 1–2 yr | after the initial presentation. | Complications (may be the presenting event) | Acute complications result primarily from | hypertension and acute renal dysfunction | . Hypertension is seen in | 60% of patients | and may be associated with | hypertensive encephalopathy in 10% | of cases. | Other potential complications | Heart failure, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, acidosis, seizures and uremia. | Medical emergencies in APSGN | A. Hyperkalemia • B. Hypertensive encephalopathy • C. Congestive heart failure • D. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN)
05 | Diagnosis | Urine analysis, serum C3, and evidence of invasive streptococcal infection establish the diagnosis.

Section 05 | Diagnosis — Urine Analysis & Complement | Urine analysis demonstrates | Color: | smoky red or cola like color | Volume: | oliguria or may be anuria with high specific gravity | Dysmorphic RBCs | RBCs casts | Nephritic range proteinuria | Polymorphonuclear leukocytes | Serum complement | The | serum C3 level | is usually | reduced in the acute phase | and returns to normal | 6–8 wk after onset | .

Section 05 | Evidence of Invasive Streptococcal Infection | A | positive throat culture | report may support the diagnosis or may simply represent the | carrier state | . | A | rising antibody titer | to streptococcal antigen(s) confirms a recent streptococcal infection. | ASOT | is commonly elevated after a pharyngeal infection but | rarely increases after skin infections | . | The best single antibody titer to document | cutaneous | streptococcal infection is the | deoxyribonuclease (DNase) B antigen | . | The clinical diagnosis of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is quite likely in a child presenting with: | Acute nephritic syndrome | Evidence of recent streptococcal infection | Low C3 level

Section 05 | Renal Biopsy — When to Consider | Renal biopsy should be considered only in the presence of: | Acute kidney injury and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN). | Nephrotic range proteinuria. | Absence of evidence for streptococcal infection. | Normal complement levels. | Persistent hematuria, proteinuria, diminished renal function, and/or a low C3 level persist in more than 2 months after onset.
06 | Differential Diagnosis & Prevention | The differential diagnosis includes many of the causes of hematuria; prevention targets the family contacts.

Section 06 | Differential Diagnosis & Prevention | Differential diagnosis | The differential diagnosis of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis includes | many of the causes of hematuria | — e.g., IgA nephropathy, membranoproliferative GN, lupus nephritis, Henoch–Schönlein purpura nephritis, and other post-infectious causes (see Hematuria deck). | Prevention | Early | systemic antibiotic therapy | for streptococcal throat and skin infections does | NOT eliminate | the risk of glomerulonephritis. | Family members | of patients with acute glomerulonephritis should be | cultured | for group A β-hemolytic streptococci and | treated if culture positive | .
07 | Treatment | General measures during the oliguric phase, plus specific management of renal insufficiency, hypertension and the infection.

Section 07 | Treatment of APSGN | A) General measures | Bed rest: | only indicated during the | oliguric phase | of illness. | Fluid restriction: | Fluid intake = | UOP + 400 ml / m² | of body surface area. | Protein and salt restriction | . | High carbohydrate diet | to provide adequate calories. | B) Specific measures | Management of the | acute effects of renal insufficiency and hypertension | . | Eradication of streptococcal infection | by a | 10-day course | of systemic antibiotic therapy with | penicillin | — antibiotic therapy does not affect the natural history of glomerulonephritis.

Section 07 | Prognosis | Complete recovery occurs in | more than 95% | of children with acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. | Mortality in the acute stage can be | avoided | by appropriate management of acute kidney injury, cardiac failure, and hypertension. | Infrequently the acute phase may be severe and lead to | glomerular hyalinization and chronic renal insufficiency | . | Recurrences are extremely rare | .

Wrap-Up | Key Takeaways | APSGN = acute, specific, self-limited GN after group A β-hemolytic streptococcal infection: gross hematuria, edema, hypertension, oliguria. | Throat strains 4 & 12 (winter/spring, 1–2 wk, ASO elevated) vs skin strain 49 (summer, 2–3 wk, ASO may be normal). | Immune complexes deposit as | subepithelial humps | on the GBM → edema, hypertension, oliguria. | Diagnosis: smoky/cola urine with dysmorphic RBCs and casts, nephritic proteinuria, | low C3 | , rising ASO/DNase B titers. | Emergencies: hyperkalemia, hypertensive encephalopathy, CHF, RPGN. Biopsy only for RPGN, nephrotic proteinuria, or atypical features. | Treatment: fluid = UOP + 400 ml/m², salt/protein restriction, 10-day penicillin; prognosis excellent (>95% recover, recurrence rare). | Next topic: Proteinuria — detection, classification and evaluation. | Source: Pediatric Renal Book 4th Grade — Prof. Dr. Mohamed Bahbah & Prof. Dr. Ghada Al-Mashad (pp. 67-69)

01 | Detection of Proteinuria | Three methods: urine dipstick test, 24-hour urine collection, and the urine protein/creatinine ratio.

Section 01 | Detection — Dipstick & 24-Hour Collection | Urine dipstick test | Offers a | qualitative assessment | of urinary protein excretion. | Detects primarily | albuminuria | ; less sensitive for other forms of proteinuria. | 24 hours urine collection | Upper limit of normal in healthy children: | 150 mg/24 hr (4 mg/m²/hr) | . | Abnormal | : > 4 mg/m²/hr. | Nephritic range | : 4–40 mg/m²/hr. | Nephrotic range | : more than 40 mg/m²/hr. | Dipstick reporting scale | Negative • Trace (10–20 mg/dL) • 1+ (30 mg/dL) • 2+ (100 mg/dL) • 3+ (300 mg/dL) • 4+ (1000–2000 mg/dL)

Section 01 | Detection — Urine Protein / Creatinine (Upr/UCr) Ratio | Why use the ratio? | Determination of the protein (mg/dL) / creatinine (mg/dL) ratio on a | random urine specimen | is an alternative to quantitating proteinuria, useful when a | timed urine collection is not practical | . | Normal | Ratios | less than 0.5 | in children younger than 2 yr of age and | less than 0.2 | in children 2 yr of age or older suggest normal protein excretion. | Nephritic range | A ratio between | 0.2 to 2 | suggests nephritic range proteinuria. | Nephrotic range | A ratio | > 2 | suggests nephrotic-range proteinuria.
02 | Classification & Etiology | Proteinuria in children: transient, orthostatic (postural), glomerular, and tubulo-interstitial.

Section 02 | Transient & Orthostatic Proteinuria | Transient Proteinuria — causes | Fever | Exercise | Dehydration | Cold exposure | Seizure | Orthostatic (Postural) Proteinuria | The | most common cause of persistent proteinuria | in school-aged children and adolescents — up to | 60% | of children with persistent proteinuria. | Usually | asymptomatic | ; discovered on routine urinalysis with unknown cause. | Normal or slightly increased protein in the | supine | position; in the | upright | position excretion increases | up to 10-fold, up to 1,000 mg/24 hr (1 g/24 hr) | . | Hematuria, hypertension, and renal dysfunction are absent | . | Long-term follow-up is prudent to monitor for hematuria, hypertension, diminished renal function, or proteinuria exceeding | 1,000 mg/24 hr | .

Section 02 | Glomerular Proteinuria | Causes | Acute post-infectious glomerulonephritis, Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, Mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis, Membranous nephropathy, Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, Lupus nephritis, IgA nephropathy, Henoch-Schönlein purpura nephritis, Sickle cell nephropathy | Aspect | Detail | Mechanism | Due to increased permeability of the glomerular capillary wall. | Level | Range from less than 1 g to more than 3 g / 24 hr. | Type — Selective | Loss of plasma proteins of molecular weight up to and including albumin. | Type — Nonselective | Loss of albumin and of larger molecular weight proteins such as IgG. | Associations | Hypertension, hematuria, or renal dysfunction.

Section 02 | Tubulo-Interstitial Proteinuria | Causes | Heavy metal poisoning | Cystinosis | Wilson disease | Acute tubular necrosis | Tubulointerstitial nephritis | Polycystic kidney disease | Key features | Mechanism: | injury to the proximal tubules → diminished re-absorptive capacity. | Level: | fixed low-grade proteinuria (usually < 1 g/24 hr). | Type: | low molecular weight proteins. | Associations: | glucosuria, phosphaturia, bicarbonate wasting, aminoaciduria. | Glomerular vs tubular proteinuria | Asymptomatic patients with persistent proteinuria generally have | glomerular | rather than tubular proteinuria. In occult cases, distinguish by | electrophoresis of the urine | : tubular proteinuria — little or no albumin; glomerular proteinuria — the major protein is albumin.

Section 02 | Initial Evaluation of Persistent Fixed Proteinuria | Measurement of | serum creatinine | . | 24-hr urinary protein excretion | . | Serum albumin | level. | C3 | level. | Low-grade proteinuria (150–1,000 mg/24 hr) with normal findings | Renal biopsy | may not be indicated | — the underlying process may be transient and resolving (e.g., acute post-infectious glomerulonephritis), or specific pathologic features of a chronic renal disease may not yet be apparent. | Such patients should have periodic re-evaluation consisting of | Physical examination, Blood pressure determination, Urine analysis, Measurement of serum creatinine, and 24-hr urinary protein excretion | .

Section 03 | Three Categories of AKI | 1. Prerenal AKI (prerenal azotemia) | Characterized by | diminished effective circulating arterial volume | → inadequate renal perfusion → decreased GFR. | Evidence of kidney damage is absent | . If the underlying cause of renal hypo-perfusion is reversed promptly, renal function returns to normal. If hypo-perfusion is | sustained | , intrinsic renal parenchymal damage may develop. | 2. Intrinsic renal AKI | Characterized by | renal parenchymal damage | , including sustained hypo-perfusion / ischemia. | 3. Post-renal AKI | Characterized by | obstruction of the urinary tract | . In a patient with two functioning kidneys, obstruction must be | bilateral | to result in AKI. In general, | relief of the obstruction results in recovery | of renal function — except in patients with associated | renal dysplasia | or | prolonged urinary tract obstruction | .

Intrinsic renal (renal parenchymal damage) | Glomerulonephritis: | Post-infectious / post-streptococcal, Lupus erythematosus, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, Membranoproliferative, Anti-glomerular basement membrane, Hemolytic-Uremic syndrome | Acute tubular necrosis: | Cortical necrosis, Renal vein thrombosis | Acute interstitial nephritis: | Tumor infiltration, Tumor lysis syndrome

Postrenal (urine outflow obstruction) | Obstructive lesions | Posterior urethral valve | Pelviureteric junction obstruction (PUJ) | Ureterovesicular junction obstruction | Ureterocele | Mass / stone / functional | Tumors | Urolithiasis | Hemorrhagic cystitis | Neurogenic bladder

A critically ill child with protracted hypotension and nephrotoxic medications → ATN. | Examination: | peripheral edema, rales, cardiac gallop → volume overload (GN or ATN). Rash and arthritis → SLE or HSP nephritis. | Laboratory: | specific gravity < 1010; Uosm < 350 mOsm/kg; UNa > 40 mEq/L; FENa > 2% (> 10% in neonates). | Post-renal | History: | a neonate with hydronephrosis on prenatal ultrasound and a palpable bladder → congenital urinary tract obstruction, perhaps posterior urethral valves. | Examination: | palpable flank masses → renal vein thrombosis, tumors, cystic disease, or urinary tract obstruction. | For the cause: | bladder catheterization; abdominal ultrasound to exclude obstructive uropathy. | Urinary findings that localize intrinsic AKI | 1. Hematuria, proteinuria, RBC or granular casts → | glomerular disease | . 2. WBCs and WBC casts with low-grade hematuria and proteinuria → | tubulointerstitial disease | . 3. Section 06 | Other Findings That Help in Diagnosis | Anemia | — usually dilutional or hemolytic (SLE, renal vein thrombosis, HUS); | leukopenia | (SLE); | thrombocytopenia | (SLE, renal vein thrombosis, HUS). | Serum | C3 may be consumed | in post-infectious, SLE, or membranoproliferative GN; antibodies detected to streptococcal (post-streptococcal GN), nuclear (SLE), neutrophil cytoplasmic (ANCA — Wegener granulomatosis, microscopic polyarteritis), or GBM (Goodpasture disease) antigens. | Chest radiography | may reveal cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion (fluid overload). | Renal ultrasonography | may reveal hydronephrosis and/or hydroureter, suggestive of urinary tract obstruction. | Renal biopsy | may ultimately be required to determine the precise cause of AKI in patients who do not have clearly defined prerenal or post-renal AKI.

Section 07 | Treatment of AKI | Hospitalization | All children with AKI require hospital care for monitoring of fluid balance, electrolytes and renal function. | Medical management — treatment of the cause | Restore circulating volume in prerenal AKI; treat the underlying disease (e.g., antibiotics for infection, steroids/immunosuppression for GN); relieve obstruction in post-renal AKI. | Correction of electrolyte and acid-base disturbances | Manage hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, acidosis, hyperphosphatemia/hypocalcemia; adjust fluids and drugs as renal function changes.

Indwelling dialysis catheters. | Neurological symptoms (fatigue, poor concentration, headache, drowsiness, memory loss, seizures, peripheral neuropathy) | Uremic factor. Aluminum toxicity. Hypertension. | Gastrointestinal symptoms (feeding intolerance, abdominal pain) | Gastro-esophageal reflux. Decreased gastrointestinal motility. | Hypertension | Volume overload. Excessive renin production. | Hyperlipidemia | Decreased plasma lipoprotein lipase activity. | Pericarditis / cardiomyopathy | Uremic factor(s). Hypertension. Fluid overload. | Glucose intolerance | Tissue insulin resistance.

Section 05 | Laboratory Findings Include | Elevations in | blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine | . | Hyperkalemia | . | Hyponatremia | (if volume overloaded). | Acidosis | . | Hypocalcemia | . | Hyperphosphatemia | . | Elevation in | uric acid | . | Patients with heavy proteinuria may have | hypoalbuminemia | . | Normochromic normocytic anemia | . | Serum | cholesterol and triglyceride | levels are usually elevated. | CKD from | glomerulonephritis | : urinalysis shows | hematuria and proteinuria | . | CKD from | congenital lesions | (renal dysplasia): urinalysis usually has a | low specific gravity | and | minimal abnormalities | .
06 | Treatment | Replace absent/diminished renal functions and slow the progression of renal dysfunction.

Section 06 | Treatment — Overview & Monitoring | Aims of treatment | 1. | Replacing absent/diminished renal functions | , which progressively increase in parallel with the progressive loss of GFR. 2. | Slowing the progression | of renal dysfunction. | Care setting & monitoring | Children with CKD should be treated at a medical center capable of supplying | multidisciplinary services | — medical, nursing, social service, nutritional, and psychological support. Management requires close monitoring of the patient's clinical and laboratory status. | Blood studies to be followed routinely | Hemoglobin level and serum electrolytes • Blood urea nitrogen, creatinine • Calcium, phosphorus, albumin, and alkaline phosphatase | Periodic studies | PTH levels and radiographic studies of bone | — early evidence of renal osteodystrophy. | Echocardiography | — to identify left ventricular hypertrophy and cardiac dysfunction.

Section 06 | Fluid & Electrolyte Management and Acidosis | Fluid and electrolyte management | Most children maintain | normal sodium and water balance | with the sodium intake derived from an appropriate diet. | High blood pressure, edema, or heart failure → | sodium restriction and diuretic therapy | . | Fluid restriction | is rarely necessary until ESRD requires dialysis. | Potassium balance | is maintained until renal function deteriorates to the level at which dialysis is initiated. | Hyperkalemia | may develop with excessive dietary potassium, severe acidosis, or hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism (destruction of the renin juxtaglomerular apparatus). | Hyperkalemia treatment: | restrict dietary potassium | , | oral alkalinizing agents | , and/or | Kayexalate | . | Acidosis | Metabolic acidosis develops in | almost all children | with CKD — decreased net acid excretion by the failing kidneys. | Either | Bicitra (1 mEq sodium citrate/ml) | or | sodium bicarbonate tablets (650 mg = 8 mEq of base) | may be used to maintain serum bicarbonate | above 22 mEq/L | .

Section 06 | Nutrition & Growth | Nutrition | Dietary | phosphorus, potassium, and sodium | restricted according to the individual patient's laboratory studies and fluid balance — to provide the recommended dietary allowance of caloric intake for age. | Protein intake: 2.5 g/kg/24 hr | , of high biologic value — eggs and milk, followed by meat, fish. | Water-soluble vitamins, zinc and iron | supplements only if deficiencies are confirmed. Supplementation with fat-soluble vitamins | A, E, and K | is usually not required. | Growth — short stature | Short stature is one of the | most significant long-term sequelae | of childhood CKD. | Key etiologic factor: a | growth hormone (GH)-resistant state | — elevated GH levels but | decreased IGF-I levels | and major abnormalities of IGF-binding proteins. | Children who remain | less than −2 SD for height | despite optimal medical support (adequate caloric intake, effective treatment of renal osteodystrophy, anemia, and metabolic acidosis) may benefit from | recombinant human growth hormone (rHuGH) | . | rHuGH | 0.05 mg/kg/24 hr | subcutaneously, with periodic dose adjustment to achieve normal height velocity for age. | rHuGH may be continued until the patient: | 1. Reaches the | 50th percentile for midparental height | , 2. Achieves a | final adult height | , or 3. Undergoes | renal transplantation | .

Section 06 | Renal Osteodystrophy & Anemia | Renal osteodystrophy | A | spectrum of bone disorders | in CKD. Most common in children: | high-turnover bone disease | from secondary hyperparathyroidism — skeletal pathology: | osteitis fibrosa cystica | . | Clinical: | muscle weakness, bone pain, fractures with minor trauma; in growing children — rachitic changes, varus and valgus deformities of long bones, slipped capital femoral epiphyses. | Laboratory: | ↓ serum calcium, ↑ serum phosphorus, ↑ alkaline phosphatase, normal PTH; radiographs of hands, wrists, knees → subperiosteal resorption with widening of the metaphysis. | Treatment: | prevent bony deformity and normalize growth velocity — low phosphorus diet and phosphate binders. | Anemia & vitamin D therapy | Anemia: | primarily | inadequate erythropoietin production | ; usually manifest at | GFR < 35 mL/min/1.73 m² | . Recombinant human erythropoietin ( | rHuEPO | ) has dramatically decreased the need for transfusion. | Vitamin D therapy | is indicated with: 1. Renal osteodystrophy with PTH levels | > 3× the upper limit of normal | , or 2. Persistent hypocalcemia despite reduction of serum phosphorus | below 6 mg/dL | .

Section 06 | Hypertension & Immunization | Hypertension | Hypertensive children with suspected | volume overload | : | salt-restricted diet (2–3 g/24 hr) | and may benefit from | loop diuretic (furosemide) | therapy. | ACE inhibitors (enalapril, lisinopril) | are the antihypertensive medication of | choice | in cases of CKD associated with | proteinuria | . | Immunization | Children with CKD should receive | all standard immunizations | according to the schedule used for healthy children. | Live vaccine is contraindicated | during treatment with immunosuppressive medications.

Section 06 | Adjustment in Drug Dosage & Renal Replacement Therapy | Adjustment in drug dosage | Many drugs are excreted by the kidneys → | dosing may need to be adjusted | to maximize effectiveness and minimize toxicity. | Strategies: | lengthening the interval | between doses, | decreasing the absolute dose | , or both. | GFR = | 0.413 × (length in cm / serum creatinine (mg/dL)) | — modified | Schwartz formula | . | Renal replacement therapy | In the form of | hemodialysis | or | peritoneal dialysis | , in | stage 5 CKD | or | end-stage renal disease | .

Wrap-Up | Key Takeaways | CKD = kidney structure/function abnormality or GFR < 60 ml/min/1.73 m² for > 3 months (KDOQI). | Staging: 1 (>90) → 2 (60–89) → 3 (30–59) → 4 (15–29) → 5 (<15 = ESRD). | Etiology by age: <5 yr — congenital (hypoplasia/dysplasia, obstructive uropathy); >5 yr — glomerular diseases and inherited disorders. | Progression driven by hemodynamic perturbations, hypertension, proteinuria, podocyte injury, cytokines, profibrotic factors. | Findings: uremia, acidosis, Na/K disorders, renal osteodystrophy, growth retardation, anemia, bleeding, infection, neurological/GI symptoms, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, cardiomyopathy, glucose intolerance. | Management: fluids/electrolytes, Bicitra/bicarbonate (HCO₃ > 22), protein 2.5 g/kg/24 hr, rHuGH (−2 SD), phosphate binders + vitamin D, rHuEPO, ACE inhibitors, dose adjustment (Schwartz formula), dialysis at stage 5. | Next topic: Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs) in children. | Source: Pediatric Renal Book 4th Grade — Prof. Dr. Mohamed Bahbah & Prof. Dr. Ghada Al-Mashad (pp. 81-87)

01 | Prevalence & Etiology | UTI occurs in 3–5% of girls and 1% of boys — an important risk factor for renal insufficiency.

Section 01 | Prevalence | Urinary tract infections (UTI) occur in | 3–5% of girls | and | 1% of boys | . | In girls, the first UTI usually occurs by the age of | 5 yr | , with peaks during | infancy and toilet training | . | After the first UTI, | 60–80% of girls | will develop a second UTI within | 18 mo | . | Most UTIs of boys occur during the | 1st yr of life | ; UTIs are | much more common in uncircumcised boys | . | The prevalence varies with age: during the 1st yr of life, the | male:female ratio is 2.8–5.4:1 | . Beyond 1–2 yr, there is a striking female preponderance, with a | male:female ratio of 1:10 | . | UTIs have been considered an | important risk factor | for the development of renal insufficiency or end-stage renal disease.

Section 01 | Etiology — Causative Organisms | Escherichia coli | The | main cause | of urinary tract infections in children. | Klebsiella & Proteus | Follow | E. coli | in frequency. | Staphylococcus saprophyticus | A pathogen in | both sexes | . | Viral infections | Particularly | adenovirus | , may also occur. | Clinical importance | UTIs have been considered an | important risk factor | for the development of | renal insufficiency or end-stage renal disease | .
02 | Clinical Manifestations & Classification | There are three basic forms of UTI: pyelonephritis, cystitis, and asymptomatic bacteriuria.

Section 02 | Pyelonephritis | Characterized by any or all of the following: | abdominal or flank pain, fever, malaise, nausea, vomiting | , and occasionally | diarrhea | . | Some | newborns and infants | may show nonspecific symptoms such as | jaundice, poor feeding, irritability, weight loss | . | Involvement of the renal parenchyma is termed | acute pyelonephritis | , whereas if there is no parenchymal involvement, the condition may be termed | pyelitis | . | Acute pyelonephritis may result in | renal injury | , which is termed | pyelonephritic scarring | .

Section 02 | Cystitis & Asymptomatic Bacteriuria | Cystitis | Cystitis indicates | bladder involvement | . | Symptoms include: | dysuria, urgency, frequency, suprapubic pain | . | Incontinence | and | malodorous urine | . | Cystitis | does not cause fever | and | does not result in renal injury | . | Asymptomatic bacteriuria | Individuals with a | positive urine culture | without any manifestations of infection. | Occurs | almost exclusively in girls | . | This condition is | benign | and | does not cause renal injury | .
03 | Pathogenesis & Risk Factors | Nearly all UTIs are ascending infections from the fecal flora.

Section 03 | Pathogenesis | Bacteria arise from the fecal flora | → | Colonize the perineum | → | Enter the bladder via the urethra | → | Ascend to the kidney → acute pyelonephritis | Hematogenous spread | In rare cases, renal infection may occur by | hematogenous spread | . | Risk factors | Female • Uncircumcised male • Vesicoureteral reflux • Toilet training • Voiding dysfunction • Obstructive uropathy • Urethral instrumentation • Tight clothing (underwear) • Pinworm infestation • Constipation • Anatomic abnormality (e.g., labial adhesion) • Neuropathic bladder
04 | Diagnosis | Urine culture is necessary for confirmation and appropriate therapy.

Section 04 | Diagnosis — Laboratory | General principle | A UTI may be suspected based on the | symptoms | or findings on | urinalysis | , or both, but a | urine culture is necessary | for confirmation and appropriate therapy. | With acute renal infection | Leukocytosis | , | neutrophilia | , and elevated | erythrocyte sedimentation | and | C-reactive protein | are common. | With a renal abscess | The | white blood cell count is markedly elevated | to | greater than 20,000 to 25,000/mm³ | . | Blood cultures | Because | sepsis is common in pyelonephritis | , particularly in infants and in any child with obstructive uropathy, | blood cultures should be considered | .

Section 04 | Imaging Studies & VCUG | Imaging studies | Goal: identify | anatomic abnormalities | that predispose to infection. | Renal ultrasonogram | — to rule out hydronephrosis and renal or perirenal abscess; may show acute pyelonephritis (in | 30–60% of cases | ) by demonstrating an enlarged kidney. | Power Doppler ultrasonography | — slightly more sensitive but unreliable in identifying all cases. | Voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) | in a | young infant male | with a past history of a urinary tract infection. | The most common finding is | vesicoureteral reflux | ; when the diagnosis of acute pyelonephritis is uncertain, | renal scanning with technetium-labeled DMSA or glucoheptonate | is useful. | If vesicoureteral reflux is present, a | DMSA scan | often is performed to assess whether | renal scarring | is present. | A voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) is also indicated in | All children | younger than 5 yr | with a UTI. | Any child with a | febrile UTI | . | School-aged girls | who have had | two or more UTIs | . | Any male | with a UTI.
05 | Treatment | Treat cystitis promptly; use broad-spectrum tissue-level antibiotics for pyelonephritis.

Section 05 | Treatment — Acute Cystitis | Principle | Acute cystitis should be treated | promptly | to prevent its possible progression to | pyelonephritis | . | Situation | Treatment | Severe symptoms | A specimen of bladder urine is obtained for culture and | treatment is started immediately | . | Mild symptoms (results of culture available) | A | 3-to-5-day course | of therapy with | trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole | is effective against most strains of | E. coli | . | Alternative 1 | Nitrofurantoin (5–7 mg/kg/24 hr in three to four divided doses) | — effective, and active against | Klebsiella-Enterobacter | organisms. | Alternative 2 | Amoxicillin (50 mg/kg/24 hr) | — effective as initial treatment but has no clear advantages over the sulfonamides or nitrofurantoin.

Section 05 | Treatment — Acute Febrile Pyelonephritis | Principle | In acute febrile infections suggestive of pyelonephritis, a | 14-day course of broad-spectrum antibiotics | capable of reaching significant tissue levels is preferable antibiotic therapy. | Agent | Details | Parenteral ceftriaxone | 50–75 mg/kg/24 hr | , not to exceed | 2 g | . | Ampicillin + aminoglycoside | Ampicillin | 100 mg/kg/24 hr | with | gentamicin 3–5 mg/kg/24 hr | . | Aminoglycoside precautions | Potential | ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity | ; serum creatinine and | trough gentamicin levels | before treatment and daily thereafter. | Aminoglycosides & Pseudomonas | Particularly effective against | Pseudomonas | ; | alkalinization of urine | with sodium bicarbonate increases their effectiveness in the urinary tract. | Oral third-generation cephalosporins | Cefixime | — as effective as parenteral ceftriaxone against a variety of gram-negative organisms | other than Pseudomonas | .

Section 05 | Abscess, Obstruction & Prophylaxis | Surgical / percutaneous drainage | Children with a | renal or perirenal abscess | or with infection in | obstructed urinary tracts | require | surgical or percutaneous drainage | in addition to antibiotic therapy and other supportive measures. | Prophylaxis | Prophylaxis against | re-infection | using either the | sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim combination | or | nitrofurantoin | at | one third of the normal therapeutic dose once a day | — often effective. | Prophylaxis with | amoxicillin | or | cephalexin | also may be effective.

Wrap-Up | Key Takeaways | UTI occurs in 3–5% of girls and 1% of boys; M:F = 2.8–5.4:1 in infancy, 1:10 beyond 1–2 yr. | Main organism: | E. coli | , then Klebsiella/Proteus, S. saprophyticus, adenovirus. | Three forms: pyelonephritis (fever, flank pain — causes scarring), cystitis (dysuria/urgency — no renal injury), asymptomatic bacteriuria (benign, girls). | Pathogenesis: ascending infection from fecal flora via urethra; risk factors include female sex, VUR, uncircumcised male, voiding dysfunction. | Diagnosis: urine culture confirms; WBC > 20,000–25,000/mm³ with abscess; blood cultures in infants/obstructive uropathy. | Imaging: renal ultrasound, VCUG (<5 yr, febrile UTI, ≥2 UTIs in school-aged girls, any male), DMSA for scarring. | Treatment: cystitis — TMP-SMX 3–5 days or nitrofurantoin; pyelonephritis — 14 days ceftriaxone or ampicillin + gentamicin (monitor levels), cefixime orally; drainage for abscess/obstruction. | Prophylaxis: TMP-SMX or nitrofurantoin at 1/3 therapeutic dose daily; amoxicillin or cephalexin alternative. | End of the Pediatric Nephrology series — all 9 topics complete. | Source: Pediatric Renal Book 4th Grade — Prof. Dr. Mohamed Bahbah & Prof. Dr. Ghada Al-Mashad (pp. 87)
